description:
Cyber threats like Q-Day and entropic warfare are emerging with a new technilogical era. Our old methods of security are vulnerable. That's where EISD comes in. Entropy as Infrustructure for Security and Defense is a new, hacker-created field striving to keep us safe.

#EISD #quantum #entropy SAMANTHA LOWRIMORE, known as CyberSamantha, is an ethical hacker, entropy advocate, founder of PostQuantSec.io, and one of the first recognized quantum hackers working to secure life beyond Earth and the quantum horizon. A cybersecurity engineer, her work begins with quantum-era security and extends beyond, spanning quantum cybersecurity, AI, blockchain, satellites, and interplanetary computing. She is helping to build the foundations that will safeguard the next generation of human and machine intelligence across worlds. Through her research and pioneering of the Lowrimore Approach to Quantum Migration, she is redefining how global leaders understand security, resilience, and ethics at the edge
title: The imminent encryption crisis | Samantha Lowrimore | TEDxUniversityofMississippi

author: TEDx Talks
description: Marc Byrnes asks one question three times, and by the third time you realize he is asking about you. Battery chargers empower the people around them; battery drainers want to be king of the castle. Six decades of mentors, setbacks, a company rebuilt around one word, and one formula: IQ minus EQ equals Miss Q. Marc Byrnes is Chairman Emeritus of Oswald Companies, one of the country's largest employee-owned insurance brokers, which he led beginning in 1996, rebuilding a 103-year-old firm of 40 people around one word, caring, and growing it into 1,400 employee-owners. He has chaired the United Way of Greater Cleveland and serves on the boards of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and University School, and Inside Business has named him one of the 100 most influential leaders in Northeast Ohio. He is University School Class of 1972, and at 72 he coaches the school's freshman football team. His talk asks one question three times: are you a battery charger, or a battery drainer? His answer draw
title: Are you a battery charger? | Marc Byrnes | TEDxHunting Valley

author: TEDx Talks
description: Nationally, two-thirds of people released from prison are rearrested within three years. At EDWINS, the number is a fraction of that. Chef Brandon Chrostowski shares the engine behind it: nobody is asked what they did, only who they want to become, and every base need, from an ID to housing to childcare, is covered. Same human, same prison, different engine, different result. Brandon Chrostowski trained as a chef and sommelier in Paris, New York, and Chicago before founding EDWINS Leadership and Restaurant Institute in Cleveland, which gives formerly incarcerated adults free culinary and hospitality training alongside housing, childcare, a fitness center, a butcher shop, a bakery, and a diner. Its tablet-based curriculum now reaches prisons in 49 states with more than 70,000 graduates, and its alumni return to prison at a fraction of the national rate. He is a CNN Hero and a James Beard Impact Award honoree, and the documentary about his work, Knife Skills, was nominated for an Academ
title: Breaking Out | Brandon Chrostowski | TEDxHunting Valley

author: TEDx Talks
description: On the first day of ninth grade, James Mason Jr. walked into English class with six months of memorized vocabulary, ready to prove that how you say something matters most. The praise never came, so he kept adjusting, building a different James for every room. Drawing on W.E.B. Du Bois, he draws the line between adaptation, which lets us connect, and conformity, which asks us to disappear. James Mason Jr. is a senior at University School, one of ten elected House Prefects, State Runner-Up in Poetry Out Loud, a Sherman Prize finalist, a state qualifier in the shot put, and a graduate of the inaugural Cleveland Cavaliers Social Impact Academy. His talk, “It's About What You Say, Not How You Say It,” begins on the first day of ninth grade, with six months of memorized vocabulary and a teacher's praise that never came. From there he traces code switching, the different James he built for every classroom, to W.E.B. Du Bois's 1903 idea of double consciousness, and draws a hard line between a
title: It’s About What You Say, Not How You Say It | James Mason Jr. | TEDxHunting Valley

Caring for others changes us. But what happens when we carry too much of other people's pain?

Vicarious trauma is the emotional impact of repeated exposure to the suffering of others. Often associated with first responders and helping professionals, its effects can extend into everyday life, quietly changing how we see safety, trust, relationships, and hope.

Drawing from fifteen years in anti-human trafficking work, Melissa Kaiser explores what it means to absorb other people's pain over
title: The Cost of Caring | Melissa Kaiser | TEDxFargo

author: TEDx Talks
description: Why is your quality as a neighbor measured in inches of grass? Because two developers in the 1800s told you so. Gage Martin follows the false need from the suburban lawn to product placement, the beauty industry, and the manufactured need for constant connection, and offers a rule of thumb for spotting the needs somebody sold you. Gage Martin is a senior at Louisville High School and president of a speech and debate team he has competed on for seven years, ranking among the top competitors in Ohio. He is a member of the Ohio Department of Health's Teen Wellness Team and the creator of the nationally recognized Duck Game, digging into corporate influence on culture. His talk, “The Ads on Your Phone Are Making You Mow Your Lawn,” starts with his neighbor Mr. George and a question: why is your quality as a neighbor measured in inches of grass? The answer runs from two 19th-century developers who marketed the lawn as status, through philosopher Herbert Marcuse's idea of false needs, to pr
title: The Ads on Your Phone Are Making You Mow Your Lawn | Gage Martin | TEDxHunting Valley

author: TEDx Talks
description: A phone at 4 percent, a DoorDash order, a charger at the hotel door in thirty minutes: it felt like magic. Priyasha Ghosal asks who the magician really is, and shows how friction cannot be erased, only moved onto the people we no longer have to see. Her answer is intentional friction: a three-second pause between wanting something and tapping for it. Priyasha Ghosal is a sophomore at Hawken School. At twelve she founded Light of Love, a 501(c)(3) supporting pediatric cancer patients at St. Jude and Rainbow Babies. She is a nationally recognized math competitor, a competitive dancer, and a national debate semifinalist, and she led sixteen teens to raise more than $22,000 for cardiac disease awareness in eight weeks. Her talk, “The Human Cost of Convenience,” starts with a 9:32 PM DoorDash order and asks who the magician behind instant gratification really is. Her argument: friction cannot be erased, only moved, and what we call convenience is human labor we no longer have to witness. S
title: The Human Cost of Convenience: How Efficiency Erodes Empathy | Priyasha Ghosal | TEDxHunting Valley

author: TEDx Talks
description: Voters are supposed to pick their politicians. In redistricting, politicians pick their voters. Claire Witalec shows how packing and cracking quietly decide elections before a ballot is cast, why both parties do it, and what an ordinary citizen can actually do about it, starting this week. Claire Witalec is a rising junior at Laurel School in Shaker Heights, Ohio. She is a Democracy Summer Fellow, a research intern at the Matriots, the founder of Laurel's Girl Up chapter, and a Lincoln-Douglas debater working to grow young people's civic participation and turnout. She has cold-emailed Ohio state legislators with questions about voting and representation, and they met with her. Her talk, “Where Do We Draw the Line?,” traces gerrymandering from an 1812 Massachusetts map to the districts drawn around today's voters, shows how both parties use packing and cracking to pick their own electorates, and argues that redistricting is not a Democrats versus Republicans issue but a people versus p
title: Where do we draw the line? Gerrymandering and democracy | Claire Witalec | TEDxHunting Valley

author: TEDx Talks
description: A 19th-century war over islands of bird guano, a German chemist who pulled fertilizer out of thin air, and the same molecule turned into weapons: half the people alive owe their existence to Fritz Haber’s ammonia, and millions died from it. Jackson Sarver traces the double life of one invention and asks whether our moral progress can keep pace with our technical progress, from chlorine gas to the dead zone that returns to Lake Erie every summer. Jackson Sarver is a senior at Aurora High School, a four-year varsity golfer, Student Council President, and a lover of science and history. His talk, “Feed Billions, Kill Millions,” follows the strangest thread in modern chemistry: a 19th-century war fought over islands of bird guano, the German chemist Fritz Haber whose ammonia synthesis now feeds roughly half the people on Earth, and the same molecule's dark record in chemical warfare, industrial disaster, and the dead zones that return to Lake Erie every year. It is a story about the race
title: Feed billions, kill millions: The tragedy of Fritz Haber | Jackson Sarver | TEDxHunting Valley

author: TEDx Talks
description: It starts with a fight every parent knows: "Five more minutes, Dad." Stephan de Moraes battles his kids over screens almost daily — until one evening it hits him: this was never about screen time, it's about depth. Reading for pleasure has fallen 3% a year for two decades; PISA scores are sliding across the OECD. He's convinced we're entering a "post-literate society," trading deep reading for scrolling — and warns that a shallow society isn't just uninformed, it's controllable. So when he fights his kids about their phones, he's really fighting for their freedom to think. "We fight them because we love them," he says. "We fight them because we are fighting for them." Stephan de Moraes is the Founder and Managing Partner of Índico Capital Partners, Portugal's leading venture capital and sustainability firm. A visionary investor with a global outlook, he has backed seven unicorns and served as President of APCRI, Advisor to the European Commissioner for Science and Innovation, and a Yo
title: Love, Depth, and Democracy | Stephan de Moraes | TEDxMarvila

author: TEDx Talks
description: Valerie Corcias hands the room five color cards and asks: if love had a color, what would yours be? Hands rise — a rainbow of answers. She used to think color was just a design tool, until a fisherman in a Brazilian village told her why he painted his house blue and his boat yellow: "blue protects me, yellow gives me light." That answer sent her down a decade-long path into the neuroscience of color — a client who burst into tears the moment she truly felt a color she thought she hated, research spanning 64 countries showing we feel color more alike than we think. Her conclusion: color isn't something we see, it's something we carry. She closes by asking the room to look at their card once more — and reveals her own color of love: yellow. Valerie Corcias is a pioneer in emotional color intelligence, exploring how color shapes emotion, perception, and human connection. With over 20 years of experience, she co-created the global PANTONE UNIVERSE brand and founded mycoocoon and Wanathé L
title: Color Is Love Made Visible | Valerie Corcias | TEDxMarvila

author: TEDx Talks
description: Her friend and business partner had one last request before she died of cancer: she wanted her makeup done — for her own funeral. So Beatriz de Sousa Viegas found herself in a funeral home, red lipstick in hand, playing "Girls Just Wanna Have Fun" beside an open casket. Not crying. Steady. Careful. Because her friend hadn't asked for more time — she'd asked to look like herself. That moment became the seed of Oncoglam, the magazine Beatriz co-founded to help women feel beautiful through cancer treatment, and the reason she now argues that beauty was never about vanity — it's devotion, a way of saying "I still see you" when the world reduces someone to their diagnosis. Co-founder and editor-in-chief of Oncoglam, Portugal's only magazine dedicated to cancer, lifestyle, beauty, and fashion for patients, healthcare professionals, and caregivers. Aims to bring dignity, style, and humanity to a subject often shaped by purely clinical stories. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TE
title: Beatriz de Sousa Viegas | Beatriz de Sousa Viegas | TEDxMarvila

Sarah Gerald is a North Carolina native turned Nashville resident whose music blends Southern roots with modern country storytelling.

With heartfelt lyrics, infectious melodies, and a genuine spirit, Sarah has built a sound that honors country tradition while bringing a fresh voice to today’s music scene.

Her career highlights include performances at Nashville’s legendary Bluebird Cafe and Whiskey Jam, along with a feature on YouTube’s Country Rising playlist. Her latest single, “Party Anywhere,” is available now on all streaming platforms.

At TEDxCoolSprings Youth, Sarah helped close out an unforgettable evening of ideas and inspiration with a special live performance.

We were honored to have her be part of our inaugural event and to end the evening with such an authentic and memorable performance. North Carolina native turned Nashville resident, Sarah Gerald embodies the perfect blend of Southern roots and modern country. Hailing from a small town where country music was woven i
title: Live Performance by a Country Artist | Sarah Gerald | TEDxCool Springs Youth

author: TEDx Talks
description:
It starts with a question nobody can quite answer. Actor Ricardo Pereira settles into a chair and starts turning it over out loud — is love a warm cup of coffee, or only the one you make for someone else? A dog staring down the front door, waiting? A hard goodbye? He never lands on a definition, because there isn't one — only the feeling of chasing it. Then the room shifts: the 50-voice Gospel Collective choir rises into "No Greater Love," building into a joyous, reworked "This Little Light of Mine" — "This little love of mine, I'm gonna let it shine" — and the question stops being something to answer and becomes something the whole room feels together. Gospel Collective is a ~50-voice Lisbon-based choir led by singer and conductor Manuela Oliveira, formed as a collective in 2010 with roots going back to 1999. Their repertoire spans African-American gospel, black spirituals, and afrogospel, performed in English, Portuguese, and Swahili.

Recent collaborations include Dino d'Santiago f
title: OpeningShow: Ricardo Pereira&Gospel Collective | Gospel Collective . & Ricardo Pereira | TEDxMarvila

author: TEDx Talks
description:
Imagination is where every great idea begins. Before something becomes an invention, a story, a piece of art, or a dream for the future, it first exists in someone’s mind.
“The Power of Imagination” explores how our ability to imagine can help us see possibilities beyond what already exists. As children, we naturally dream, create, and ask “What if?” But as we grow older, fear of failure, expectations, and the pressure to be realistic can sometimes make us stop imagining.
This speech invites us to rediscover that sense of curiosity and wonder. It explores how imagination can help us solve problems, create new ideas, understand different perspectives, and envision a better future.
Because imagination is not simply about dreaming of what could be—it is the first step toward making what seems impossible possible. Akein Randeniya is a young and enthusiastic student from St. Anthony’s College, Kandy, with a strong passion for public speaking and drama. He enjoys expressing ideas, performin
title: The Power of Imagination | Akein Randeniya | TEDxKandy

author: TEDx Talks
description:
We’ve all been told to “find balance.” Balance between work and life. Between ambition and rest. Between taking care of others and taking care of ourselves. It’s become the modern mantra for how to survive adulthood — as if we can somehow level out the chaos of real life with the right planner, the right morning routine, or the right podcast.

But here’s the truth: balance isn’t real. At least, not in the way we talk about it. Life doesn’t sit still long enough for equilibrium. It tilts. Constantly. And while we keep chasing the idea of perfect balance, we end up exhausted — not from doing too much, but from trying to control something that can’t be controlled.

My big idea challenges this obsession with balance and reframes it around a concept I call capacity. Capacity is not about keeping things even; it’s about building the strength to handle what’s uneven. It’s the mental, emotional, and physical bandwidth we create to navigate what life actually is — unpredictable, demanding, and
title: Capacity: Reaching Untapped Strength | Ashley Fournet | TEDxCNU

author: TEDx Talks
description:
What if the greatest barrier to our future is not what we cannot do, but what we are afraid to imagine?
The Courage to Imagine Different explores the power of challenging the ideas, expectations, and limitations that shape the way we see ourselves and the world around us. From a young age, we are often encouraged to follow familiar paths—but meaningful change begins when someone dares to ask, “What if there is another way?”
This speech invites us to embrace curiosity, question assumptions, and have the courage to imagine possibilities that may seem unusual or impossible at first. Because every innovation, every breakthrough, and every meaningful change begins as an idea that someone was brave enough to imagine.
The future belongs not only to those who know the answers, but also to those courageous enough to ask different questions. Thenuli Mehansa Vitharana is a young creative voice from Hillwood College, Kandy, with a deep passion for Arts and Music. A curious and expressive young sp
title: The courage to imagine different | Thenuli Mehansa Vitharana | TEDxKandy

author: TEDx Talks
description: Every few weeks, my phone buzzes with a familiar message: “A new software update is available.” Without thinking, I hit download. I know if I don’t, the apps will start crashing, the system will lag, and soon it won’t work the way it should. One thing has remained on my mind every time I perform an update to my phone. We update our devices all the time, yet most of us haven’t updated ourselves in years. We still run on old versions of who we used to be. Old habits. Old fears. Old ways of thinking. My big idea is simple: humans are not meant to be finished products. We’re built for continuous updates. I call this idea “Human 2.0 - The Upgrade Never Ends" Karsten Schenkelberg is a senior at CNU studying Finance hailing from Yorktown, Virginia. He is an Honors student actively involved in the Captain’s Educational Enrichment Fund, as well as a brother of the Sigma Phi Epsilon fraternity. He plans to pursue entrepreneurial ventures post graduation, and is currently developing a company wi
title: Why humans are always updating | Karsten Schenkelberg | TEDxCNU

author: TEDx Talks
description: There is no single timeline for success. Tiffany challenges how we recognize potential and what it really means to be "behind," Tiffany Minnie Wright is a Brooklyn-born Human Resources specialist at Lenovo, where she leads workplace investigations, advises global leaders, and focuses on employee experience and ethics. She is a nontraditional graduate of Fayetteville State University, earning her Business Administration degree while working full-time and raising a family. Now based in North Carolina with her husband and three children, Tiffany is also a writer, spoken word poet, and lifelong storyteller who is passionate about advancing equity in the tech industry and expanding access to opportunity for all. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx
title: There Is No Expiration Date On Ambition | Tiffany Wright | TEDxParrish Street

author: TEDx Talks
description:
We’ve all heard the saying “it takes a village.” It’s a comforting idea: the notion that a community naturally rises up around us, supporting our growth and shaping who we become. But somewhere along the way, that phrase has become a little passive. We wait for the village. We assume it will just appear. And when it doesn’t, many of us feel isolated, overwhelmed, or convinced that we’re supposed to navigate adversity alone. This talks compels us to reframe the focus. We all want a village of support during hard times, but how often do we show up as villagers for other people? 
 McKenna is a current student at Christopher Newport University studying Political Science with minors in Communication and Leadership Studies. She is deeply committed to building community, amplifying student voices, and fostering meaningful dialogue. McKenna aims to create environments where people feel seen, supported, and inspired. She is passionate about advocacy, service, and using leadership as a tool for
title: It takes a villager | McKenna Findley | TEDxCNU

On paper, Khaliah O. Guillory had built the life she always dreamed of. A former NCAA Division I basketball team captain, she carried the same drive into corporate America, where she managed a billion-dollar portfolio, led high-performing teams, and checked every box that defined success. Yet beneath the accomplishments was a question she could no longer ignore: Why did achieving more never feel like enough?

In this deeply personal TEDx talk, Khaliah shares how childhood rejection shaped decades of overachievement and how one unexpected practice helped her reconnect with herself. Through personal
title: The power of a nap | Khaliah O. Guillory | TEDxThird Ward Salon
